PHIL 1.desc: A general introduction to some of the fundamental questions, texts, and methods of philosophy. Multiple topics will be covered, and may include the existence of God, the nature of mind and body, free will, ethics and political philosophy, knowledge and skepticism. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 10.desc: Basic concepts and techniques in both informal and formal logic and reasoning, including a discussion of argument, inference, proof, and common fallacies, and an introduction to the syntax, semantics, and proof method in sentential (propositional) logic. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 100.desc: A study of Socrates and/or Plato through major dialogues of Plato. Possible topics include the virtues and happiness; weakness of the will; political authority and democracy; the theory of Forms and sensible flux; immortality; relativism, skepticism, and knowledge. May be repeated for credit with change of content and approval of instructor. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 100.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 101.desc: A study of major issues in Aristotle’s works, such as the categories; form and matter; substance, essence, and accident; the soul; virtue, happiness, and politics. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 101.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 102.desc: A study of selected texts from the main schools of Hellenistic philosophy—Stoicism, Epicureanism, and Skepticism. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 102.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 104.desc: The major writings of one or more of the seventeenth-century rationalists—Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz. Topics include the existence of God, the mind-body problem, free will, the nature of knowledge, belief, and error. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 104.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 105.desc: A study of one or more figures from seventeenth- and/or eighteenth-century philosophy, such as Bacon, Descartes, Hobbes, Cavendish, Conway, Spinoza, Locke, Malebranche, Leibniz, Astell, Berkeley, Du Chatelet, Hume, or Reid. The focus may be on particular texts or intellectual themes and traditions. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 105.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 106.desc: A study of selected portions of The Critique of Pure Reason and other theoretical writings and/or his major works in moral theory. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 106.pre: PHIL 32 or 33 or 104 or 105 or 111 or 112 or consent of instructor.

PHIL 107.desc: A study of one or more of Hegel’s major works, in particular, The Phenomenology of Spirit and The Philosophy of Right. Readings and discussion may also include other figures in the Idealist tradition—such as Fichte, Hölderlin, and Schelling—and critics of the Idealist tradition—such as Marx and Kierkegaard. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 107.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 108.desc: A study of one or more figures in nineteenth-century philosophy, such as Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, Marx, Emerson, Thoreau, Goldman, Luxemburg, James, and Mill. The focus may be on particular figures or intellectual themes and traditions. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 108.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 109.desc: Central texts, figures, and traditions in analytic philosophy. Figures may include Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Carnap, Moore, Austin, Quine, and Anscombe. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 109.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 110.desc: An examination of ancient Greek philosophy, focusing on major works of Plato and Aristotle. PHIL 10, PHIL 111, and PHIL 112 should be taken in order. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 110.pre: upper-division standing and department stamp or consent of instructor.
PHIL 110.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 111.desc: An examination of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century philosophy, focusing on major works of Descartes, Locke, and Hume. PHIL 110, PHIL 111, and PHIL 112 should be taken in order. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 111.pre: PHIL 110, upper-division standing and department stamp or consent of instructor.

PHIL 112.desc: An examination of late eighteenth and nineteenth-century philosophy, focusing on major works of Kant and Hegel. PHIL 110, PHIL 111, and PHIL 112 should be taken in order. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 112.pre: PHIL 111, upper-division standing and department stamp or consent of instructor.

PHIL 115.desc: This course provides an introduction to the techniques of philosophical inquiry through detailed study of selected philosophical texts and through extensive training in philosophical writing based on those texts. Enrollment limited and restricted to majors; must be taken for letter grade. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 12.desc: Strategies of scientific inquiry: how elementary logic, statistical inference, and experimental design are integrated to evaluate hypotheses in the natural and social sciences. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 120.desc: The syntax, semantics, and proof-theory of first order monadic and polyadic predicate logic. In this course, we will learn how to determine whether arguments that can be represented in first order predicate logic are deductively valid, how to symbolize English arguments, the rules of a natural deduction system, how to apply those rules to determine the logical status of symbolized arguments, and how to use semantic methods for determining validity and invalidity. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

PHIL 122.desc: Topics vary from year to year. They include Metalogic (Mathematical Logic), Modal Logic, Foundations of Logic, Foundations of Set Theory, Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems, and others. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 123.desc: Philosophical issues underlying standard and nonstandard logics, the nature of logical knowledge, the relation between logic and mathematics, the revisability of logic, truth and logic, ontological commitment and ontological relativity, logical consequence, etc. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

PHIL 124.desc: The character of logical and mathematical truth and knowledge; the relations between logic and mathematics; the significance of Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorem; Platonism, logicism, and more recent approaches. May be repeated for credit three times with change of content.

PHIL 125.desc: A survey of theories of rational inference and rational choice, covering topics in probability and decision theory, formal epistemology, and statistics. This course provides an introduction to formal methods widely used in contemporary philosophy. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 125.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 126.t: Topics in the History of Logic
PHIL 126.desc: Problems and figures in history of logic. Subject matter varies, in some cases a single author or text (e.g., Aristotle, The Port Royal Logic, Leibniz, Kant, Frege, Tarski), in others a particular tradition or problem (e.g., Hilbert’s Program, intuitionism, quantification, logicism and psychologism, modality). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

PHIL 13.desc: An inquiry into the nature of morality and its role in personal or social life by way of classical and/or contemporary works in ethics. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 130.desc: Central problems in metaphysics, such as free will and determinism, the mind-body problem, personal identity, causation, primary and secondary qualities, the nature of universals, necessity, and identity. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 130.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 131.desc: An in-depth study of some central problem, figure, or tradition in metaphysics. May be repeated for credit with change of content and approval of instructor. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 131.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 132.desc: Central problems in epistemology such as skepticism; a priori knowledge; knowledge of other minds; self-knowledge; the problem of induction; foundationalist, coherence, and causal theories of knowledge. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 132.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 134.desc: Examination of contemporary debates about meaning, reference, truth, and thought. Topics include descriptional theories of reference, sense and reference, compositionality, truth, theories of meaning, vagueness, metaphor, and natural and formal languages. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 134.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 134.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 136.desc: Different conceptions of the nature of mind and its relation to the physical world. Topics include identity theories, functionalism, eliminative materialism, internalism and externalism, subjectivity, other minds, consciousness, self-knowledge, perception, memory, and imagination. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 136.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 136.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 137.desc: The nature of action and psychological explanation. Topics include action individuation, reasons as causes, psychological laws, freedom and responsibility, weakness of will, self-deception, and the emotions. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 137.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 138.desc: A study of the nature and significance of responsibility. Possible topics include freedom, determinism, and responsibility; moral luck; responsibility and reactive attitudes such as blame and forgiveness; responsibility and situationism; moral and criminal responsibility; responsibility and excuse; insanity and psychopathy, immaturity, addiction, provocation, and duress. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 138.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 139.desc: Social justice issues as they arise across the borders of nation-states. Topics may include nationalism and cosmopolitanism, theories of just war and just warfare, issues of migration and immigration, global distributive justice and fair trade, and international cooperation in the face of global problems such as climate change and human rights violations. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 139.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 14.t: Introduction to Philosophy: The Nature of Reality
PHIL 14.desc: A survey of central issues and figures in the Western metaphysical tradition. Topics include the mind-body problem, freedom and determinism, personal identity, appearance and reality, and the existence of God. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 140.desc: Investigation into the nature of free will, including arguments for and against its compatibility with a scientific picture of the world and competing accounts of the metaphysics of free will. Possible topics include disputes about the nature of free will; what it is for agents to cause actions; the nature of abilities or capacities to act; the relevance of neuroscience to accounts of free will; whether free will skepticism is a stable view; and experimental research on free will. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 140.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 141.desc: This course considers whether human life has meaning, and, if so, what meaning it has and under what conditions such meaning may be secured. Negative proposals considered include that life is nothing but suffering, that it is absurd, that it has no meaning. Positive proposals considered include that meaning derives from free choices, from just being, from some passion, from something transcendent, or from human relationships or purposeless play or knowledge or achievement or morality. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 141.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 142.desc: The nature, function, and value of emotion. Topics include theoretical approaches to defining (and distinguishing particular) emotions; the roles of emotions in structuring perception, cognition, and action; the rationality of emotion; morality and the emotions; emotions and mental/social well-being; and specific emotions such as fear or grief. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 142.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 142.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 143.desc: The nature and function of perception. Topics include theoretical approaches to defining (and distinguishing particular) perceptual modalities; informational interactions within and between these modalities, and between perception and thought; the roles of perception in justifying knowledge about the world and guiding both thought and action; and the nature of perceptible qualities (colors, sounds, smells, tastes). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 143.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 145.desc: Central problems in philosophy of science, such as the nature of confirmation and explanation, the nature of scientific revolutions and progress, the unity of science, and realism and antirealism. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 145.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 146.desc: Philosophical problems in the development of modern physics, such as the philosophy of space and time, the epistemology of geometry, the philosophical significance of Einstein’s theory of relativity, the interpretation of quantum mechanics, and the significance of modern cosmology. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 146.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 147.desc: Philosophical problems in the biological sciences, such as the relation between biology and the physical sciences, the status and structure of evolutionary theory, and the role of biology in the social sciences. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 147.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 147.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 148.desc: Investigation of ethical and epistemological questions concerning our relationship to the environment. Topics may include the value of nature, biodiversity, policy and science, and responsibility to future generations. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 148.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 149.desc: Philosophical issues raised by psychology, including the nature of psychological explanation, the role of nature versus nurture, free will and determinism, and the unity of the person. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 149.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 15.t: Introduction to Philosophy: Knowledge and Its Limits
PHIL 15.desc: A study of the grounds and scope of human knowledge, both commonsense and scientific, as portrayed in the competing traditions of Continental rationalism, British empiricism, and contemporary cognitive science. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 150.desc: Theoretical, empirical, methodological, and philosophical issues at work in the cognitive sciences (e.g., psychology, linguistics, neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and computer science), concerning things such as mental representation, consciousness, rationality, explanation, and nativism. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 150.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 151.desc: An introduction to elementary neuroanatomy and neurophysiology and an examination of theoretical issues in cognitive neuroscience and their implications for traditional philosophical conceptions of the relation between mind and body, perception, consciousness, understanding, emotion, and the self. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 151.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 152.desc: Philosophical issues of method and substance in the social sciences, such as causal and interpretive models of explanation, structuralism and methodological individualism, value neutrality, and relativism. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 152.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 153.desc: An examination of one or more philosophical issues pertaining to animals. Topics will vary and may address animal ethics, animal minds, animals in the philosophy of science or conservation, metaphysical or epistemological questions related to animals, or the treatment of animals in a particular tradition or period in the history of philosophy. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 153.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 153.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 155.desc: Introduction to Mexican philosophy with discussion of the work of such figures as Las Casas, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz, Vasconcelos, Uranga, Zea, Villoro, Dussel, Hierro, Lara, and Hurtado. Topics may include historical movements, such as scholasticism, positivism, Mexican existentialism, and indigenous thought, as well as contemporary developments and the relationship to philosophy in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 155.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 156.desc: Philosophical issues surrounding Latina/o/x peoples, which may include debates about the nature, function, and stability of this identity; social and political issues, such as immigration, economics, racial politics, and justice; phenomenological and existential accounts of latinidad; Latina feminism; and the relationship of these concerns to other philosophical traditions. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 156.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 157.t: Topics in Latin American and Latinx Philosophy
PHIL 157.desc: A study and in-depth analysis of one or more figures or themes in Latin American or Latina/o/x/e philosophy. The focus may be on particular topics (liberation, indigeneity, immigration, the idea of regional or ethno-philosophy), figures (for example, Sor Juana, Vasconcelos, Mariategui), or themes in historical or contemporary philosophy (such as Mexican existentialism, philosophy of liberation, Latina feminism). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.

PHIL 158.desc: A study of one or more highly influential figures from Chinese philosophy, such as Confucius, Mozi, Mencius, Laozi, Zhuangzi, Xunzi, Han Feizi, and later Chinese thinkers. The focus may be on particular texts or intellectual themes and traditions. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 158.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 159.desc: An examination of foundational questions about morality, including issues such as ethical objectivity; the relation between science and ethics; metaphysical, epistemological, and semantic issues about ethics; moral expertise; moral conflict; moral motivation; morality and practical reason; and the rational authority of morality. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 159.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 159.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 16.desc: An introduction to philosophy which uses science fiction to make abstract philosophical problems vivid. Science fiction themes may include time travel, teleportation, virtual reality, super-intelligent robots, futuristic utopias, and parallel universes. These scenarios raise philosophical questions about knowledge, reality, ethics, and the mind. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 160.desc: Systematic and/or historical perspectives on central issues in ethical theory such as deontic, contractualist, and consequentialist conceptions of morality; rights and special obligations; the role of happiness and virtue in morality; moral conflict; ethical objectivity and relativism; and the rational authority of morality. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 160.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 161.t: Topics in the History of Ethics
PHIL 161.desc: Central issues and texts in the history of ethics. Subject matter can vary, ranging from one philosopher (e.g., Confucius, Aristotle, Kant, or Mill) to a historical tradition (e.g., Greek ethics or the British moralists). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 161.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 162.desc: An examination of contemporary moral issues, such as abortion, euthanasia, war, affirmative action, and freedom of speech. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 162.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 163.desc: Moral issues in medicine and the biological sciences, such as patient’s rights and physician’s responsibilities, abortion and euthanasia, the distribution of health care, experimentation, and genetic intervention. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 163.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 164.desc: Philosophical issues involved in the development of modern science, the growth of technology, and control of the natural environment. The interaction of science and technology with human nature and political and moral ideals. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 164.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 165.desc: Examination of freedom and equality under the US Constitution, focusing on Supreme Court cases concerning discrimination on grounds of race, ethnic background, gender, undocumented status, wealth, and sexual orientation, and cases regarding contraceptives, abortion, interracial marriage, polygamy, and same-sex marriage. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 165.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 166.desc: Central issues about the justification, proper functions, and limits of the state through classic texts in the history of political philosophy by figures such as Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Marx, and Arendt. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 166.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 167.desc: Different perspectives on central issues in contemporary political philosophy, such as the nature of state authority and political obligation, the limits of government and individual liberty, liberalism and its critics, equality and distributive justice. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 167.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 167.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 168.desc: A study of issues in analytical jurisprudence such as the nature of law, the relation between law and morality, and the nature of legal interpretation and issues in normative jurisprudence such as the justification of punishment, paternalism and privacy, freedom of expression, and affirmative action. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 168.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 168.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 169.desc: Philosophical examination of core concepts and theses in feminism, feminist philosophy, and critiques of traditional philosophical approaches to morality, politics, and science, from a feminist perspective. May also treat the historical development of feminist philosophy and its critiques. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 169.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 170.desc: A philosophical investigation of the topics of race and racism. The role of “race” in ordinary speech. The ethics of racial discourse. Anthropological and biological conceptions of race. The social and political significance of racial categories. Post-racialist conceptions of race. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 170.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 171.desc: An in-depth analysis of one or more issues in philosophy of law. Topics might include legal positivism and natural law, legal and constitutional interpretation, judicial review within a constitutional democracy, First Amendment jurisprudence, substantive due process and equal protection, the limits of the criminal law, responsibility and punishment, psychiatry and the law, and the moral foundations of civil law. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 171.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 172.desc: An in-depth analysis of a central problem, figure, or tradition in political philosophy. Topics may include minority rights, war and peace, political philosophy as it pertains to animals or the environment, immigration, ideal vs. non-ideal theory, or a detailed examination of a contemporary thinker or school of political thought. Content may vary. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 172.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 173.desc: An in-depth exploration of an issue in bioethics. Topics will vary, and may include the ethics of genetic engineering, mental capacity and genuinely informed consent, the just distribution of health care, the ethics of geo-engineering, and the ethics of climate change and health. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 173.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 173.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 174.desc: A survey of ethical issues arising in the collection, storage, analysis, consolidation, and application of data. Topics may include data as property and public resource, privacy and surveillance, data and discrimination, algorithms and fairness, and data regulation. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 174.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 175.desc: Central issues in philosophical aesthetics such as the nature of art and aesthetic experience, the grounds of artistic interpretation and evaluation, artistic representation, and the role of the arts in education, culture, and politics. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 175.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 176.desc: This course examines the nature of culture, its significance, and its varied meanings. Topics may include case studies of culture’s relationship to psychology, politics, media, religion, and the arts. Course may include discussion of related questions concerning culture and race, class, nationalism, sexuality, and gender. Contemporary and classical readings, drawing from philosophy, anthropology, sociology, literature, religion, and related fields. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 176.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
PHIL 176.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 177.desc: A study of philosophical themes contained in selected fiction, drama, or poetry, and the philosophical issues that arise in the interpretation, appreciation, and criticism of literature. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 177.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 178.desc: Careful, line-by-line translation of passages of intermediate difficulty from German philosophical texts, both classic (Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Schopenhauer) and contemporary (Heidegger, Wittgenstein, Habermas). P/NP grades only. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content. LIGM 1D or equivalent level of study recommended.

PHIL 179.desc: Continuation of PHIL 178 in the careful, line-by-line translation of passages of advanced difficulty from German philosophical texts, both classic (Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Schopenhauer) and contemporary (Heidegger, Wittgenstein, Habermas). May be repeated for credit three times with change of content .
PHIL 179.pre: consent of instructor or completion of PHIL 178.

PHIL 180.desc: An examination of the phenomenological tradition through the works of its major classical and/or contemporary representatives. Authors studied will vary and may include Brentano, Husserl, Heidegger, Stein, Merleau-Ponty, Levinas, and Irigaray. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 180.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 181.desc: Classical texts and issues of existentialism. Authors studied will vary and may include Nietzsche, Kierkegaard, Heidegger, Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Fanon. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 181.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 183.desc: The focus will be on a leading movement in continental philosophy (e.g., the critical theory of the Frankfurt school, structuralism and deconstruction, postmodernism) or some particular issue that has figured in these traditions (e.g., freedom, subjectivity, historicity, authenticity). May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 183.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 184.desc: This course may include topics in the philosophy of film, such as the nature of the cinematic medium, the aesthetic qualities of film, when film is art, how film is different from other artistic forms, the role of emotion, imagination, and thought in our experience of films, and why we enjoy horror and tragic movies. It may also discuss the philosophy in film by exploring how cinema engages with topics such as agency, responsibility, personal identity, justice, happiness, love, gender, etc. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 184.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 185.desc: A general introduction to the philosophy of religion through the study of classical and/or contemporary texts. Among the issues to be discussed are the existence and nature of God, the problem of evil, the existence of miracles, the relation between reason and revelation, and the nature of religious language. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 185.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 186.desc: This course analyzes the nature of authoritarianism, how it operates, what its consequences are, and what it justifies in response, by drawing from political philosophy, normative ethics, epistemology, legal philosophy, philosophy of psychology, and social philosophy. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
PHIL 186.pre: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 189.desc: Intensive application of ethics through contemporary moral dilemmas focused on developing oral and presentation skills in philosophy. Students will have the opportunity to join the department’s Ethics Bowl team for an annual national competition series. May be repeated for credit eight times with change of content.
PHIL 189.pre: upper-division standing and consent of instructor.
PHIL 189.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 191A.desc: Independent study by special arrangement with and under the supervision of a faculty member, including a proposal for the honors essay. An IP grade will be awarded at the end of this quarter; a final grade will be given for both quarters at the end of 191B.

PHIL 191B.desc: Continuation of 191A: independent study by special arrangement with and under the supervision of a faculty member, leading to the completion of the honors essay. A letter grade for both 191A and 191B will be given at the end of this quarter.

PHIL 195P.desc: Under the supervision of an instructor, undergraduate students gain teaching experience through practical experiences in course management and effective teaching methods. Pedagogy and learning apprentices must have a minimum overall grade point average of 3.0. A student may not apprentice more than once for the same course for credit or for more than one course in the same quarter. May be repeated for credit two times.
PHIL 195P.pre: upper-division standing and consent of instructor.
PHIL 195P.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 199.desc: Directed individual study by special arrangement with and under the supervision of a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.) May be repeated for credit four times with change of content and approval of instructor.
PHIL 199.res: Limited to class level: Junior, Senior

PHIL 2.desc: An exploration of paradoxes on a wide range of philosophical topics, including time, logic, science, belief, decision, and value. Paradoxes serve as a stepping stone to deeper philosophical questions, such as: Is time real? What is a person? Does language shape reality? Is infinity coherent? Can we know anything? How do we learn from experience? Are our experiences real? What is it to be rational? Should we believe in God? Can morality be rationalized? And finally, why is death bad? May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 200.desc: Introduction to philosophical methods of analysis through study of classic historical or contemporary texts. Writing intensive. Enrollment limited to philosophy entering graduate students.

PHIL 201A.desc: A study of selected texts or topics in the history of philosophy. Usually the focus will be on a single major text. May be taken for credit nine times with changed content.

PHIL 202.desc: An introduction to some central issues in ethical theory with emphasis on classic texts or contemporary authors. May be taken for credit three times with changed content.

PHIL 204A.t: Core Course in Philosophy of Science
PHIL 204A.desc: An introduction to one or more central problems in the philosophy of science, or in the philosophy of one of the particular sciences, such as the nature of confirmation and explanation, the nature of scientific knowledge, reductionism, the unity of science, or realism and antirealism. May be taken for credit three times with changed content.

PHIL 205A.desc: An introduction to central topics in metaphysics with emphasis on classic texts or contemporary authors. May be taken for credit three times with changed content.

PHIL 206A.desc: An introduction to central topics in epistemology with emphasis on classic texts or contemporary authors. May be taken for credit three times with changed content.

PHIL 207.t: Core Course in Philosophy of Mind
PHIL 207.desc: An introduction to central topics in philosophy of mind with emphasis on classic texts or contemporary authors. May be taken for credit three times with changed content.
PHIL 207.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 208.t: Core Course in Philosophy of Language
PHIL 208.desc: An introduction to central topics in philosophy of language with emphasis on classic texts or contemporary authors. May be taken for credit three times with changed content.
PHIL 208.pre: graduate status or consent of instructor.

PHIL 209A.desc: Study and discussion of classic work in history of science, sociology of science and philosophy of science, and of work that attempts to develop a unified science studies approach. Required for all students in the Science Studies Program.

PHIL 209B.desc: Study and discussion of selected topics in the science studies field. Required for all students in the Science Studies Program. May be repeated as course content changes annually.

PHIL 209C.t: Colloquium in Science Studies Part I
PHIL 209C.desc: A forum for the presentation and discussion of research in progress in science studies, by graduate students, faculty, and visitors. Required for all students in the Science Studies Program. May be repeated as course content changes annually.
PHIL 209C.pre: enrollment in the Science Studies Program.

PHIL 209D.t: Introduction to Science Studies Part II
PHIL 209D.desc: Continuing the introduction developed in part I, this course examines recent key topics and problem situations in science studies. Emphasis is on recent theoretical perspectives and empirical studies in communication, history, philosophy, and sociology of science and technology, and the interplay between them. May be taken for credit up to six times. Students may receive a combined total of twenty-four units for ANTH 269, COGR 225D, HIGR 241, PHIL 209D, and SOCG 255D.

PHIL 210.desc: A study of selected texts or topics from the history of Greek philosophy. Usually centers on works by Plato or Aristotle. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 214.desc: A study of selected texts or topics from philosophers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, or Locke. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 215.desc: A study of selected texts or topics from philosophers of the eighteenth century: for example, Kant or Hume. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 216.desc: A study of selected texts or topics from philosophers of the nineteenth century: for example, Hegel, Mill, or Nietzsche. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 218.desc: A study of the historical development of the analytical movement, with emphasis on major texts. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 220.desc: Contemporary debates on the nature of agency, responsibility, and freedom. May include questions about free will and determinism, intentional action, group agency, culpability, and the significance of recent scientific findings on these topics. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 222.desc: A study of selected issues in the philosophy of logic. The focus may be on contemporary texts or historical works or both. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 230.desc: Topics may include identity, personal identity, universals and particulars, modality and possible worlds, causation, reduction, supervenience, freedom and determinism, space and time, and realism versus antirealism. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 232.desc: This seminar will cover issues such as rival accounts of knowledge, justification, and warrant, traditional and contemporary perspectives on empiricism, rationalism, and pragmatism, and skepticism. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 234.desc: Central issues in contemporary philosophy of language, such as the nature of linguistic meaning, truth, content, reference, the syntax and semantics of various linguistic constructions, presupposition, speech acts, the epistemology of language understanding and language learning, the mental/psychological basis of linguistic understanding and use. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 236.desc: Contemporary debates on the nature, function, and operation of the mental. May include questions about the mind-body relation, mental causation, perception, consciousness, and mental representation. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 24.desc: The differences among good science, bad science, and pseudoscience. Topics include the philosophical and practical demarcation problems; science and values; probabilistic fallacies, cognitive biases, and perceptual illusions; causation versus correlation, the placebo effect; why and when science is trustworthy; and case studies ranging from ESP to homeopathy to climate change denialism. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 245.desc: This seminar will cover current books and theoretical issues in the philosophy of science. May be taken for credit seven times with changed content.

PHIL 246.desc: Systematic problems and historical and contemporary perspectives on foundational issues in physics. May include issues in the philosophy of space and time, the interpretation of relativity theory and quantum mechanics, or the foundations of statistical mechanics and probability. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.
PHIL 246.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 247.desc: Historical and contemporary perspectives on foundational issues about biology. May include questions about the nature of biological explanation, the relation of biology to chemistry and physics, the status of attributions of function, and the relation of biology to the social sciences. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 25.t: Science, Philosophy, and the Big Questions
PHIL 25.desc: An inquiry into fundamental questions at the intersection of science and philosophy. Topics can include Einstein’s universe; scientific revolutions; the mind and the brain. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 250A.desc: Contemporary debates about the study of the mind-brain as studied in one or more of the empirical cognitive sciences. May include questions about the different strategies of explanation invoked, the conceptions of representation employed, the connections between theoretical models developed. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 256.desc: Contemporary or historical approaches to philosophy in or concerned with Latin America. May focus on particular countries (e.g., Mexico, Peru), specific time periods (e.g., the nineteenth century), particular topics or movements (e.g., political liberalism, the philosophy of liberation), or specific figures (e.g., Alberdi, vaz Ferreira, Castellanos). May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 26.desc: An exploration of the interaction between scientific theory and practice on the one hand, and society and values on the other. Topics can include the relationship between science and religion, global climate change, DNA, medicine, and ethics. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 260.desc: Topics may include metaethics (e.g., the semantics, metaphysics, epistemology, and normativity of ethics), consequentialism and deontology, moral psychology (e.g., freedom, responsibility, and weaknesses of will), or substantive moral problems. The approach may be systematic, historical, or both. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 263.desc: An examination of moral issues in medicine and the biological sciences, such as patient’s rights and physician’s responsibilities, abortion and euthanasia, the distribution of health care, experimentation, and genetic intervention. May be taken for credit four times with changed content.

PHIL 267.desc: Topics may include the nature and limits of state authority, liberty and equality, distributive justice, liberalism and its critics (e.g., feminists, libertarians, and others), or issues in jurisprudence. The focus may be on classic texts or contemporary authors. May be taken for credit six times with changed content.

PHIL 27.desc: An examination of ethical principles (e.g., utilitarianism, individual rights, etc.) and their social and political applications to contemporary issues: abortion, environmental protection, and affirmative action. Ethical principles will also be applied to moral dilemmas in government, law, business, and the professions. Warren College students must take course for a letter grade in order to satisfy the Warren College general-education requirement. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 27.pre: CAT 2 and 3 or CAT 2CE and 3CE or CCE 1 and 2 or DOC 2 and 3 or HUM 1 and 2 or MCWP 40 and 50 or MCWP 40R and 50R or MMW 12 and 13 or WCWP 10A and B or SYN 1 and 2 or WARR 11A and 11B or SYN 1R and 2R.

PHIL 271.t: Agency, Morality, and Psychology Research Group
PHIL 271.desc: This course is designed for students to gain feedback from students and faculty on works in progress on the topics of agency, morality, and psychology, and on contemporary research on these topics. The course is suitable for those specializing in moral psychology, agency, ethics, and philosophy mind and psychology, and for those with special interests in the topics.

PHIL 275.desc: This course meets regularly to discuss primary or secondary literature in the area of German philosophy (including Kant, Fichte, Hegel, etc.). The reading is designed both for students doing active research in the field and for those seeking to gain some familiarity with it. Nongraduate students may enroll with consent of instructor. S/U grades only. May be taken for credit twenty-one times with changed content.

PHIL 277.desc: This course meets biweekly with students reading and presenting material from the phenomenological literature. The course is designed both for students doing active research in phenomenology and for those seeking to gain some familiarity with that tradition. Can be taken nine times for credit with changed content.

PHIL 278.t: Topics and Methods in Contemporary Philosophy
PHIL 278.desc: Investigation of central issues in contemporary philosophy. Content varies but typically will center on a recent and important philosophical book. Can be taken nine times for credit with changed content.

PHIL 28.desc: An examination of a single set of major contemporary social, political, or economic issues (e.g., environmental ethics, international ethics) in light of ethical and moral principles and values. Warren College students must take course for a letter grade in order to satisfy the Warren College general-education requirement. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 280.t: Philosophy of Science Topics and Methods
PHIL 280.desc: This course meets weekly to discuss recent books or articles in philosophy of science. The reading is designed both for students doing active research in the field and for those seeking to gain some familiarity with it. Can be taken nine times for credit with changed content.
PHIL 280.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 281.t: History of Philosophy Research and Methods
PHIL 281.desc: This course meets to discuss work in progress in the history of philosophy. Its aim is to introduce understanding of the methods and standards of research in the field through constructive criticism of each other’s work. Can be taken nine times for credit with changed content.

PHIL 282.desc: Weekly or biweekly meetings to discuss recent literature in ethics, broadly construed so as to include ethical theory, normative ethics, jurisprudence, and historical traditions in these fields. The course is suitable for those specializing in ethics and for those seeking some familiarity with the field. Can be taken nine times for credit with changed content.

PHIL 283.t: Topics and Methods in Latin American Philosophy
PHIL 283.desc: This course is designed for students to gain feedback from students and faculty on works in progress on Latin American philosophy. The course is suitable for those specializing in historical and contemporary philosophy in Latin America and for those with special interests in the topics.

PHIL 284.desc: A research group for graduate students engaged in philosophy or history of the biological sciences. The group discusses biological, historical, and philosophical articles and books and ongoing research projects. Can be taken nine times for credit with change of content.
PHIL 284.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 285.desc: Focused examination of specific problems or themes in some area of philosophy. May be taken for credit nine times with changed content.

PHIL 286.desc: A research group for graduate students engaged in philosophy or history of the physical sciences. The group discusses physical, historical, and philosophical articles and books and ongoing research projects. Can be taken nine times for credit with change of content.
PHIL 286.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 287.desc: This group provides training in reading and translating philosophical Greek by having students prepare translations of passages and lead discussions. The group helps train graduate students preparing for Departmental Greek Exam. Can be taken nine times for credit with change of content.
PHIL 287.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 288.desc: This group provides training in reading and translating philosophical Latin by having students prepare translations of passages and lead discussions. The group helps train graduate students preparing for departmental Latin exam.
PHIL 288.pre: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

PHIL 290.desc: Supervised study of individually selected philosophical topics. S/U grades permitted.

PHIL 292.desc: Each enrolled student produces a research essay ready for publication, presents it to students and faculty, and offers critiques of other students’ presentations. Units will vary according to enrollment in course. To be taken in fall quarter of third year of philosophy graduate study.

PHIL 295.desc: Advanced individual research studies under the direction of a member of the staff. Hours of outside preparation will vary with number of units taken. May be taken for credit nine times with changed content.

PHIL 31.desc: A survey of classical Greek philosophy with an emphasis on Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, though some consideration may be given to Pre-Socratic and/or Hellenistic philosophers. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 32.t: Philosophy and the Rise of Modern Science

PHIL 35.desc: An exploration of central philosophical issues as they have been taken up in the diverse philosophical traditions of the Americas, such as indigenous philosophy, Latin American philosophy, American Pragmatism, and the Civil Rights movement, among others. Topics may include ethics, social and political philosophy, colonialism, philosophy of race and gender, environmentalism, and issues in philosophy of language. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 35.res: Limited to class level: Freshman, Junior, Sophomore, Senior

PHIL 50.desc: A survey of philosophical issues concerning law and society, such as the rule of law, the moral limits of the law, individual rights, judicial review in a constitutional democracy, the justification of punishment, and responsibility. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 500.desc: A course designed to satisfy the requirement that graduate students should serve as teaching assistants, either in the Department of Philosophy or in one of the writing programs offered by the various colleges. Each PhD candidate must teach the equivalent of quarter time for three academic quarters. Students are permitted to sign up as TAs for a maximum of eighteen quarters.

PHIL 51.desc: This course will address the complex moral challenge of climate change. Topics include ethical values in climate modeling; the moral psychology of climate change; individual versus structural approaches to decarbonization; global justice and the distribution of greenhouse gas emissions; the ethics of geoengineering; decolonization and the climate crisis; discounting and obligations to future generations. May not be repeated for credit.
PHIL 51.res: Limited to class level: Freshman, Junior, Sophomore, Senior

PHIL 55.desc: As our physical and digital lives increasingly merge, we face new challenges in understanding how to think about both worlds. This course will examine many philosophical issues and challenges that arise as our world rapidly becomes more digital. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 60.desc: This course will focus on philosophical topics surrounding love and sex by examining both historical and contemporary texts. We will discuss love and sex from a number of different angles and perspectives, and focus on issues such as the nature of love both as a mental and social phenomenon; different kinds of love and their demands on us; the connection between love and sex; the ethics and politics of love, sex, and marriage; and sex and consent. May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 65.desc: This course explores how language and power intersect by critically examining the often unnoticed ways that our language reflects, reinforces, and reshapes the power structures that surround us. Examples of questions discussed include: How does power influence ideas about what is the “right” way to speak? How do in-group and out-group uses of slurs differ? How does language reflect and reinforce social stereotypes? Should our language change in order to promote social aims, and if so, how? May not be repeated for credit.

PHIL 87.desc: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students. May be repeated for credit four times with change of content.

PHIL 90.desc: An investigation of a selected philosophical topic through readings, discussions, and written assignments. May be repeated for credit two times with change of content.
